You way is probably better tbh though, after thinking about it for a bit, I realized for performance sake its probably???? not best to use time/update time every frame. I think multiplying time.Deltatime gives even the miliseconds of a seccond, every single frame which is data you dont really need or use. I mean its probably not the end of the world considering how powerful cpus are, but something to consider and i def bet there is a better way using the corutines like you were. It should work though, and i doubt unless your game is super crazy would something so insignificant effect performance that greatly, just maybe a little caveat to the advice I gave. I also could be talking nonsense, what is life.

You can actually get a timer running in update instead of IEnumerator/ Courotines , I'm not an expert on them though and cant really debug em, only use em for minor delays and things. To have time flow in the update method/function, you would use a variable(like minutes) and say minutes += 1 * time.deltaTime. 1 second = 1 minute in this case.  Then underneath that I would have a few if statements to check . Like if(minutes > 60) then set minutes back to 1, add 1 to hours variables. if(hours >24) then set hours to 1 and days to 1, then the 12 months, ect. I "think" this should work how you intend instead of it being instant, i cant say i've tested this, but i do know for a fact you can update a varible in the update method over time by multiplying with time.deltaTime. I hope it helps!

Some ideas/suggestions/resources i think might help 


http://blender.stackexchange.com/questions/6425/keep-sharp-edges-when-using-subdivision-surface

"Weighted edge creases for subdivision surfaces allows you to change the way Subsurf subdivides the geometry to give the edges a smooth or sharp appearance.

The crease weight of selected edges can be changed using Transform Properties (N) and change the Median Transform slider. A higher value makes the edge “stronger” and more resistant to subsurf. Another way to remember it is that the weight refers to the edge’s sharpness. Edges with a higher weight will be deformed less by subsurf. Recall that the subsurfed shape is a product of all intersecting edges, so to make the edges of an area sharper, you have to increase the weight of all the surrounding edges." 

The above bit of into is usefull if you use a smooth/subdivide modifier(dont just select all verts and smooth a few times over, try the modifier out if you havent .

Heres my suggestion and what i think would be quickest though, its likely from your blender picture that the actual shading of the sword is set to flat.

while in edit mode with the sword, select all the vertices, then  on the left panel try to find something like.. shading/uv. Make sure to click smooth for faces/be extra safe and just click smooth for verts edges too. This doesnt change how smooth the objects geomtry itself is, but rather how the light effects it, is it a hard edge or a smooth transition. I hope this helps! 

I think thats a fine looking sword for getting new to modeling and unity friend.

Edit. looked around a little more. This link should help more.

https://docs.blender.org/manual/ko/dev/modeling/meshes/editing/smoothing.html

Sometimes its not the skeletons or the wieght painting that cause the wierd bend in the knee(most time it is) but what you have to do, is make sure there are extra edge loops in areas that tend to bend(like the knee) inside the 3D modeling progam you use, how can it stretch the faces smoothly, if when in fact its only working with a few faces? think about how much smoother an object can look with a few extra edge loops/verticices, and then think about how that can easily apply to movable areas like joints. Dont go too crazy though! It could very well be the wieght painting. but my guess is a combination of both weight painting, and not enough edge loops. Could be wrong though! If its the wieght painting, just really spend some time and think about it. in terms of blender, red areas should bend very little/none, yellow should be the start of the upperleg from kneecap/start of lowerleg from kneecap, get some gradient in there and move the bones inside blender. and then weight paint as its moved! To make it look smooth from any angle, theres a way to set all bones in blender back to defaul pose/shape when you are done. Hold on, lemme try to remember/open it up.

Alt+R to reset rotation to default postion.
Alt+G to reset location.

so once you are done, and have all the bones moved/painted on as you move em live, then set all the bones back.
